question: What does the 1W/1D/4H tape say after ASX breached the $29.25 hard stop to $26.27, and how do we reconcile the facts vs. snapshot stage split?

epigraph.quote: The tape always tells the truth before the earnings consensus catches up. When price breaks below the 200-day average and your hard stop on double volume, discipline means honoring the exit without waiting for a bounce.
epigraph.author: Stan Weinstein (adapted from Secrets for Profiting in Bull and Bear Markets)

web_blocks.html: On November 20, 2026, ASX's technical tape suffered a decisive breakdown. Shares plunged -13.84% in one session to close at $26.27 on 23.70 million shares (2.13x 30-day average volume; 2.06x 20-day average on the facts ledger) [13, 14, 22]. Over the past week and month, ASX lost -27.23% (1W) and -37.63% (1M) on TradingView (-26.10% 1W / -30.39% 1M on Finviz), leaving the stock -45.19% below its $47.93 52-week high [13, 14]. Most critically, the $26.27 close sliced -$2.98 (-10.19%) below our prior $29.25 hard stop, as well as breaking Pivot S1 ($35.21), the 200-day SMA ($34.43), and Pivot S2 ($30.91) [14, 21, 22].

We must disclose a methodological split between our two automated ledgers transparently. The snapshots ledger (stage2_evaluation) classifies ASX as STAGE_4 (AVOID_STAGE4_OR_BROKEN / CAP_REJECTED) because close $26.27 trades -34.77% below the 50-day SMA ($40.27), -30.85% below the 30-week SMA ($37.99), -27.51% below the 10-week EMA ($36.24), and -23.70% below the 200-day SMA ($34.43) [14, 21]. By contrast, facts_US_2026-11-20.json outputs a mechanical stage: 1 (Stage 1 Basing) tag solely because price sits near its 63-day low ($26.06) beneath a falling 50-DMA [22]. Given 8 distribution days in 25 sessions, a -37.63% 1M crash on 2.13x volume, and zero base duration, we enforce the stricter STAGE_4 (CAP_REJECTED) classification [14, 22].

Inspecting Weekly (1W), Daily (1D), and 4-Hour (4H) charts confirms there is no confirmed bottom or institutional accumulation shelf yet. Every timeframe points downward inside a broader S&P 500 Downtrend.

web_blocks.html: Notice the options and macro confirmation. Our options desk check (options_snapshot.py) stamps NO_OPTIONS_EDGE because ASX sits far below both its 50-day ($40.27) and 200-day ($34.43) floors while carrying a CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL quality grade [21]. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 sits in a confirmed Downtrend with 10 distribution days in 25 sessions, only 34.5% of tracked stocks above their 50-day average, and only 1 of 11 sectors above their 20-day average [22]. Against a 3.04 one-year beta on the positions ledger, fighting Stage 4 momentum in a market Downtrend carries severe capital-loss risk [22, 23].

book_paragraphs: Chapter 7 showed us that ASX's reconciled $1.22 FY2027E EPS puts Base fair value at just $16.47 (at a TSMC-capped 13.5x multiple) amid negative NT$115.9 billion nine-month free cash flow, 54 percent higher debt, and new U.S. export friction. Now Chapter 8 delivers the verdict of the price tape—and on November 20, 2026, the tape is unambiguous. ASX closed at $26.27, plunging 13.84 percent in a single session on 23.70 million shares, more than double its 30-day average volume.

In just thirty days, the stock has dropped 37.63 percent on TradingView, erasing $21.66 per share—or more than 45 percent—from its $47.93 October peak. Even more important for our portfolio discipline, Friday's close sliced cleanly through every single moving average and pivot shelf we mapped a week ago: Pivot S1 at $35.21, the 200-day simple moving average at $34.43, Pivot S2 at $30.91, and our own hard invalidation stop at $29.25.

Let us address a technical detail transparently so you never feel confused by conflicting screener labels. On November 20, 2026, our daily facts ledger printed a mechanical "Stage 1 (Basing)" label because ASX closed near its 63-day low of $26.06 underneath a falling 50-day average. However, our multi-factor snapshot engine classifies ASX as Stage 4 (CAP_REJECTED, Avoid Stage 4 or Broken). Why do we enforce Stage 4? Because a true Stage 1 base requires months of sideways stabilization and drying volume. A stock crashing 13.8 percent in one day on 2.13x volume, sitting 23.7 percent below its 200-day line and 34.8 percent below its 50-day line with eight distribution days in twenty-five sessions, is in active Stage 4 markdown.

Walk across the three timeframes on your TradingView screen and you see zero sign of buyer control. On the weekly chart, ASX trades 27.5 percent below its 10-week EMA ($36.24) and 30.85 percent below its 30-week SMA ($37.99), with weekly RSI sliding to 37.77. On the daily chart, 14-day RSI sits at 30.48—technically near oversold, yet as Stan Weinstein warned decades ago, oversold stocks in Stage 4 routinely stay oversold while grinding lower toward their prior cycle shelves. On the 4-hour chart, price sits nearly 20 percent below its 20-EMA ($32.57) with 4H RSI at 24.52 and no upside turn.

Two flow statistics explain who is selling and why there is no easy short-squeeze floor underneath $26.27. First, short interest on Finviz is tiny—just 0.50 percent of the float (11.03 million shares, 1.34 days to cover). That means Friday's 23.7-million-share waterfall was not a speculative short raid that might snap back violently; it was institutional long-only liquidation adjusting to negative free cash flow and November 18 BIS export rules. Second, the entire S&P 500 has shifted into a confirmed Downtrend, with ten distribution days over the last twenty-five sessions and only 34.5 percent of tracked names above their 50-day average. For a high-beta ADR carrying a 3.04 one-year beta, every 1 percent drop in the index translates into roughly 3 percent of downside pressure.

Our options desk reached the exact same conclusion. Under our rules, we never buy calls or bullish call spreads on a stock trading below its 50-day and 200-day floors, especially one rated Cyclical Conditional rather than Compounder Pass. The options engine stamped NO_OPTIONS_EDGE. When both the equity tape and the options desk reject new exposure simultaneously, capital preservation becomes the only rational priority.

book_subsections.title: Why the Scanner Support Band ($35.70–$40.87) Became Overhead Supply
paragraphs: Notice a critical trap in automated technical screens: when a stock crashes fast enough, backward-looking support algorithms still print zones anchored to the 50-day ($40.27) and 200-day ($34.43) moving averages—roughly $35.70 to $40.87. At a $26.27 close, those former support lines have flipped into a dense ceiling of trapped buyers 36 to 56 percent above today's price.

Meanwhile, looking downward below $26.06, there is almost no recent consolidation shelf until you look all the way back toward the $13.35–$13.71 52-week low, or the $13.35–$16.00 trough zone from earlier in the cycle. That air pocket explains why trying to catch ASX here on the hope of a quick bounce is dangerous: volatility (ATR14) has widened to $2.81 per day, or 10.7 percent of the share price, with Bollinger Band width expanding to 72.3 percent.

book_subsections.title: What a Real Stage 1 Base and Stage 2 Turn Would Look Like
paragraphs: Respecting Stage 4 does not mean writing off ASE Technology's engineering achievements forever; it means refusing to hold or buy a falling knife. Before ASX could ever return to our active watchlist, three concrete technical events must unfold over months, not days.

First, selling volume must dry up as the stock carves out a multi-week sideways floor—likely inside the $14 to $18 value band—where weekly closes stop making lower lows. Second, the 4-hour and daily charts must reclaim the 50-day SMA ($40.27 currently, though that average will fall toward price over time) on expanding accumulation volume. Third, the 30-week SMA must flatten and turn higher with relative strength outperforming the S&P 500. Until those boxes check, any bounce into $29–$34 is merely an exit opportunity or a dead-cat rally into overhead supply.

book_subsections.title: Why High-Beta Semiconductors Magnify Market Downtrends
paragraphs: When evaluating a technical breakdown like ASX's 27.2 percent weekly decline to $26.27, context across the broader tape matters just as much as the individual chart. On November 20, 2026, the S&P 500 sat in an official Downtrend with ten institutional distribution days over the prior twenty-five sessions, only 34.5 percent of tracked companies holding above their 50-day moving averages, and just one out of eleven sectors holding above its 20-day line.

In a healthy bull market, an oversold daily RSI near 30 on a market leader often attracts fast institutional dip-buying. In a ten-distribution-day Downtrend, however, portfolio managers actively raise cash by selling their highest-beta, most liquid winners—and ASX carries a 3.04 one-year beta on our positions ledger. That macro pressure explains why all five semiconductor hardware and OSAT peers in our peer matrix—ASX, Amkor, TSMC, Jabil, and Celestica—dropped into Stage 4 together during November 2026.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: In Stage 4, the biggest enemy is hoping for a bounce back to your broken stop. At $26.27—nearly 24% below the 200-day average on 2.13x volume—the tape has already answered the question we asked at $35.55.
